note: Trait-blind atomic evidence episodes decomposed from rawNotes.md by the orchestrating session, before any trait taxonomy was consulted. Armstrong is unusually self-documented (extensive private tapes/letters/scrapbooks), so more raw episodes survived curation than for other candidates in this cohort -- reflected honestly rather than artificially trimmed to match.

episodes.text: As a boy, worked for the Karnofsky family (Jewish immigrant peddlers) who were consistently warm to him, lent him money toward his first cornet, and, per his own later account, "taught him how to live -- real life and determination."

In 1969, while hospitalized for a life-threatening illness, spontaneously began writing a memoir about the Karnofsky family decades after the fact, prompted only by hearing his doctor sing a Yiddish lullaby -- an unprompted act of documenting gratitude toward people who had helped him as a child.
Wore a Star of David pendant for the rest of his life as a deliberate, ongoing symbol of gratitude toward "my Jewish family" and a reminder of the poor boy he had once been.

Arrested for firing a pistol in the street on New Year's Eve 1912 and sent to the Colored Waif's Home for Boys; there, under an instructor, learned proper cornet technique and rose to lead the Home's own brass band before his release in 1914.

Worked his way up through the New Orleans music scene and Mississippi riverboats over several years, steadily building reputation and playing experience before being summoned to Chicago by mentor Joe "King" Oliver in 1922.

Married pianist Lil Hardin (1924), a trained musician herself, who actively pushed him to leave his mentor Oliver's shadow and pursue his own independent career rather than remain a sideman indefinitely.

Oliver privately admitted, per his wife Lil Hardin's later account, to deliberately keeping Armstrong close specifically to prevent him from surpassing him ("I'll still be the King") -- real competitive tension underneath an otherwise warm, publicly celebrated mentor relationship.
Left Oliver for Fletcher Henderson's New York orchestra in 1925 at his wife's urging, found the year unsatisfying, and returned to Chicago rather than persisting in the arrangement.
Back in Chicago, formed the Hot Five (later Hot Seven) under his own name, drawing several musicians directly from his old mentor Oliver's own former band.

Despite the earlier competitive tension with Oliver, in later years repeatedly gave him financial help once Oliver's own career and finances had collapsed -- the earlier competitive strain did not curdle into lasting resentment on Armstrong's side.

Arrested for marijuana possession outside a Los Angeles club (1930), spent 9 days in jail awaiting trial (in a cell with two men serving 40-45-year sentences); after sentencing (30 days with time served, suspended on condition of leaving the state), went straight back to work performing that same night.

Continued using marijuana for the rest of his life despite the arrest, and articulated a considered, explicit personal philosophy about it in his own words -- distinguishing it from alcohol, comparing it to a health practice, and writing that a fellow musician's "personal habit, I don't care."

Hired Joe Glaser as manager (1935) via a 50/50 handshake deal, deliberately delegating essentially all business control to a man with an openly shady, mob-connected reputation, specifically so he could focus purely on music rather than business pressures.

Deliberately formed the All Stars (1947) as a racially integrated group, hiring a white trombonist immediately, and explicitly framed touring an integrated band through the segregated South as active social work ("busting down barriers"), noting from his own direct observation that some segregated audiences let racial divisions recede during the music.

When a recording using a racial term triggered a public boycott in the Black press, complied by re-recording with a substituted word, but also vented open frustration during the session about being pressured to revise his own art.

Publicly criticized Josephine Baker's confrontational civil-rights protest tactics, explicitly arguing performers should let "ability speak for itself" and contrasting her approach with his own preferred strategy of pursuing integration gradually through performance and professional excellence.
Was deeply stung, per private recordings capturing his anger, by accusations from younger Black critics that his stage persona amounted to a minstrel-adjacent accommodation to white audiences.

In a hotel room in September 1957, departing sharply from his own usual public avoidance of political statements, condemned the federal government's handling of the Little Rock crisis in strikingly blunt terms directly to a reporter, calling the president "two-faced" with "no guts."

When his own manager publicly suggested he was "sorry" about the Little Rock remarks, immediately and directly contradicted that characterization and reaffirmed his position rather than letting the softened framing stand.

Explicitly chose not to participate in marches or public protests, citing the practical risk of injury to his trumpet-playing hands (his literal livelihood), and instead gave financial contributions to civil rights organizations -- defending this as his own legitimate, deliberately chosen mode of contribution.

Publicly and repeatedly attacked bebop as "modern malice" in direct response to younger musicians' own criticism of his traditional style; the feud eventually resolved into genuine friendship by 1957 despite him never incorporating bebop's musical vocabulary into his own playing.

Deliberately chose refinement over reinvention in his later playing career, spending his later years "perfecting rather than exploring" the musical language he had already created -- treated by his biographer as an appropriate, deliberate artistic choice rather than a decline.

Suffered a heart attack mid-tour in Italy (1959) and resumed touring within weeks rather than taking an extended recovery period; required intensive hospital care again in 1968 for heart and kidney trouble.

After doctors explicitly advised him not to play at all following the 1968 hospitalization, nonetheless practiced trumpet daily at home against that direct medical advice -- so established a routine that neighbors would call his wife if he skipped several days.
Had a real private temper that contradicted his warm public persona -- could "blow up at you at noon and forget about it by 1 o'clock" -- yet people close to him remained loyal despite this.

Maintained an extensive, self-driven, decades-long practice of self-documentation entirely independent of any publisher or ghostwriter -- roughly 650 reel-to-reel tapes, 5,000 photographs, 350 pages of autobiographical manuscript, 86 scrapbooks kept from 1926 onward, and hand-annotated mixtapes with his own collage artwork -- a sustained, self-initiated project of narrating his own life on his own terms.

Archive material shows deliberate, hands-on written notations on his own performance scores and substantive personal edits to lyrics in his own arrangements, indicating a craft-conscious, technically engaged relationship to his material rather than pure improvisational instinct alone.

On a private tape, stopped the playback specifically to directly correct a rival musician's public claim of having originated scat singing, for his own archive's historical record: "I don't think I'll let you get away with this!"
